issues.legal_issue: The right of private defence of the body begins when a person reasonably apprehends present and imminent danger from an unlawful attempt or threat, and continues while that apprehension lasts.
material_facts: The accused side was in possession of the disputed land.
The opposing side deliberately came to forcibly prevent or obstruct that possession and cultivation, and the obstruction was unlawful.
The courts found that the accused could reasonably apprehend imminent danger to themselves and their companions from the opposing side’s threatened assault.
issues.conclusion: The right of private defence arose upon the reasonable apprehension of imminent danger; it did not depend on the accused first sustaining a serious injury.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 102 of the Indian Penal Code, the right of private defence of the body commences when a reasonable apprehension of danger arises from an attempt or threat to commit an offence, even before the offence is committed, and continues while the apprehension lasts. The danger must be present and imminent, not remote or distant. The right protects against apprehended unlawful aggression and is preventive, not punitive. The Court also relied on G. V. Subranmanyam v. State of Andhra Pradesh for the scheme of the right of private defence.

predicates.criminal_case_involving_bodily_private_d: The proceeding concerns a criminal charge in which the accused claims a right to defend a person’s body.
predicates.unlawful_forcible_aggression_threatened: An opposing person attempted or threatened unlawful force against the accused or another person.
predicates.reasonable_imminent_danger_apprehended: The circumstances gave the accused reasonable grounds to apprehend present and imminent danger to the body.

issues.definition: When a criminal case involves bodily private defence, an unlawful threat of force, and reasonable apprehension of imminent bodily danger, the right of private defence is available for as long as that apprehension continues.

issues.legal_issue: A defensive response is not excessive merely because it uses a different weapon or causes greater injury than the injury already sustained, where the circumstances reasonably indicate a grave threat.
material_facts: The opposing side used lathis, including a blow aimed at the accused’s head, a vulnerable part of the body.
The accused sustained a superficial lathi injury to the head.
The accused used a spear against an opposing person, causing a fatal chest injury.
The opposing side’s unlawful aggression and the imminent danger it posed had been established.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in treating the spear use as excessive merely because the accused had sustained only a superficial head injury and had used greater force; the appellant’s defensive use of the spear was justified on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 100 and 102 of the Indian Penal Code govern the extent and duration of private defence. A lathi blow aimed at the head may reasonably create an apprehension of death or grievous hurt; there is no general rule that a lathi can cause only mild injury or that a person facing it cannot defend themselves with a spear. In moments of grave aggression, a person cannot be expected to calculate with exact precision the force needed to repel it. The right is defensive, and the response must be assessed in light of the circumstances of the aggression.

rule.if: bodily_private_defence_claimed and imminent_unlawful_aggression and blow_aimed_at_vulnerable_body_part and defensive_response_used_during_grave_aggression

predicates.bodily_private_defence_claimed: The accused relied on the right to defend a person’s body against unlawful aggression.
predicates.imminent_unlawful_aggression: The accused faced present and imminent unlawful force.
predicates.blow_aimed_at_vulnerable_body_part: An aggressor aimed a blow at a vulnerable part of the body, such as the head.
predicates.defensive_response_used_during_grave_agg: The accused used force while confronting grave aggression, when an exact and calm calculation of the necessary response could not reasonably be expected.

issues.definition: When a person claiming bodily private defence faces imminent unlawful aggression, including a blow aimed at a vulnerable body part, and responds during grave aggression, the response is not excessive merely because it uses a different or more dangerous weapon.

issues.legal_issue: On an appeal against acquittal, where the evidence permits two reasonable views, the trial court’s view must receive due consideration.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after considering the evidence and finding that they were entitled to exercise private defence.

The High Court agreed that the opposing party had unlawfully obstructed possession and that the accused had a right of private defence, but convicted one accused on the view that his response exceeded that right.

The Supreme Court found that the trial court’s view on private defence was not erroneous or wholly unreasonable and that the High Court’s distinction rested on an unsound assessment of the force used.
issues.conclusion: The trial court’s acquittal was not based on an erroneous or wholly unreasonable view, and the High Court’s conviction of the appellant could not stand on the stated ground.
issues.legal_principle: A High Court hearing an appeal against acquittal may reappraise the evidence, but where the evidence is capable of two reasonable views, the view taken by the trial court demands due consideration.

predicates.appeal_by_prosecution_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed a trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_acquitted_after_assessing_ev: The trial court acquitted the accused after evaluating the evidence.
predicates.evidence_supports_two_reasonable_views: The evidence is reasonably capable of supporting two different views.

issues.definition: When the prosecution appeals an acquittal entered after the trial court assessed the evidence, and the evidence supports two reasonable views, the trial court’s view deserves due consideration.
